name: Chicano Movement
summary: The Chicano Movement (El Movimiento) was the Mexican American civil rights and ethnic-revival movement of roughly 1966 to 1977. It rejected assimilation, claimed pride in a mestizo and Indigenous heritage called Chicanismo, and demanded community control of schools and institutions, restitution for past discrimination and self-determination for La Raza. Its strands ran from reformist farmworker and student activism to cultural nationalism around Aztlán and a smaller Marxist current.
scope: The movement as the New Dictionary of the History of Ideas defines it: the Chicano (later Chicana/o) movement of 1966-1977, with Chicanismo, the Plan Espiritual de Aztlán (1969) and the Plan de Santa Barbara (1969) as the texts the encyclopedias tie to it, plus the 1969 Hayward symposium where Gonzales, an Alianza representative and socialists debated a Chicano party. Where these sources show the movement divided (direct action against elections, class cooperation against class struggle) the answer is a split. It excludes Chicana feminism, Chicano nationalism as a separate entry, and the later Mexican American politics of the 1980s onward.

name: Chicana/o movement
aliases.quote: The resulting challenges and concurrent mentalities became the Chicano movement, or as it is now known in recognition of the equally important participation of Chicanas, the Chicana/o movement.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: The Plan de Santa Barbara rejects assimilation as a cost of turning away from the barrio and attacks a melting pot that dilutes cultures; the encyclopedia calls the plan the most resounding rejection of assimilationism.

class-collaboration.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán says nationalism transcends class and unites poor and professional, while symposium speakers and the dictionary entry describe a Marxist current that stressed class exploitation.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The Plan de Santa Barbara says the Anglo ethic of profit and competition must be replaced by ancestral communalism and love of beauty and justice.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: The Plan de Santa Barbara condemns the pseudo-culture of technology and materialism, and the Plan de Aztlán wants Chicano values to defeat the gringo dollar value system.

corporate-influence.rationale: Gonzales says the two parties sit on the same bank and corporate boards and share industries that profit from wars.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán demands institutions serve Chicanos "on the basis of restitution" for past economic slavery, political exploitation and denial of civil rights.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán wants institutions to provide the services needed for a full life, as restitution rather than handouts, and declares that institutions belong to the people.

decide-locally.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán demands community control of schools and of barrio institutions, and the Plan de Santa Barbara says barrio people must own the schools that serve them.

direct-action.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán calls a national school walk-out and an independent party, and symposium speakers disagree whether to use elections as a tactic, so the movement points both ways.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: The dictionary entry counts affirmative-action employment practices among the concessions the movement forced.

historical-land-claim.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán grounds the claim in forefathers who came from Aztlán, though it also says the land belongs to those who work it, so the claim is partly ancestral.

history-own-civilization.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán requires education relative to the people's own history and culture, and the Plan de Santa Barbara asks Chicanos to write their own history, anthropology and literature for Chicano Studies.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán reclaims "the land of their birth" with "hands in the soil" and vows that lands rightfully theirs will be fought for and defended; the encyclopedia ties the Chicano nation to Aztlán.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán holds that social, economic, cultural and political independence together are the only road to liberation and calls for control of the Chicano economy.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán claims sovereignty and self-determination for the Chicano nation as a group, which contradicts the view that rights belong only to individuals.

land-redistribution.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán says Aztlán belongs to those who plant and harvest, and the encyclopedia reads this as the principle that land belongs to those who work it.

land-use-tenure.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán has the community acquire land and realty for the people's welfare and says the land belongs to those who work it.

minority-language-support.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán lists bilingual education among its education goals, and the dictionary entry records partial bilingual education among the concessions the movement forced.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán says "where we are the majority, we will control", and Gonzales urges Chicano majorities to incorporate or de-annex their communities and keep their own security.

national-self-determination.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán declares the Chicano nation free and sovereign and its independence, the Plan de Santa Barbara calls community self-determination the only acceptable mandate, and the dictionary entry says the movement stressed self-determination.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The Plan de Santa Barbara requires barrio and student representatives on the committees that run programs, and the Plan de Aztlán demands community control of schools.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán calls the two parties one animal feeding at the same trough, and Gonzales sued local officials to show the public they were corrupt.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The Plan de Santa Barbara says Chicanos must write their own history and literature to survive as a cultural entity, and the Plan de Aztlán calls cultural values the moral backbone of the movement.

racial-community-economic-control.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán says economic control of Chicano lives and communities must be won by controlling their own resources; a symposium speaker extends this to self-determination for all nations and peoples.

racial-franchise.rationale: The dictionary entry says the movement pressed for democratic and voting rights and won voting and representational concessions, which a racially limited franchise would deny.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán makes nationalism the common denominator for mobilizing La Raza through independent action, and the Plan de Santa Barbara calls cultural nationalism a means of total Chicano liberation.

racial-pride.rationale: The Plan de Santa Barbara calls the word Chicano a sign of "a rebirth of pride and confidence", and the Plan de Aztlán opens on pride in a historical heritage.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The movement is defined in the encyclopedia as a civil rights movement that challenged inequality and attacked a racist social structure.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The Plan de Santa Barbara names an ethic of profit, greed and competition as what communalism must replace and ranks the people's liberation above personal achievement.

single-official-language.rationale: By demanding bilingual education and a curriculum built on Chicano culture, the Plan de Aztlán sets itself against a single-language school system.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán relies on community self-defense and Gonzales proposes placing a gun to protect the community, both against a state monopoly on arms.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: The Plan de Aztlán presents Chicanos as heirs of the people of Aztlán, and the encyclopedia says its manifesto traces La Raza to an Aztec origin.

unions-good.rationale: The dictionary entry lists unionization among the movement's lasting thrusts and the United Farm Workers among its seminal organizing forces.

missingStatements.text: Communities should control the schools that serve them.
missingStatements.rationale: Both plans demand community ownership and control of schools.

quotes.text: Community control of our schools, our teachers, our administrators, our counselors, and our programs.
The idea must be made clear to the people of the barrio that they own the schools and the schools and all their resources are at their disposal.

missingStatements.text: An ethnic community should form its own political party, independent of the established parties.
missingStatements.rationale: Both the Plan de Aztlán and Gonzales call for an independent Chicano party.

quotes.text: Creation of an independent local, regional, and national political party
We start it and call it an independent Chicano political organization.

notes: Themes searched: the movement's defining encyclopedias (New Dictionary of the History of Ideas, Encyclopedia of Race and Racism, SAGE), the Plan Espiritual de Aztlan, the Plan de Santa Barbara, the 1969 Hayward symposium; Plan of Delano, Alianza, Brown Berets, Raza Unida and Chicano Moratorium pages were read but not cited as answers because organisations' texts do not answer for the movement.
